claim: When pathogens enter the host, sensing of environmental cues activates the expression of virulence genes.
source: When pathogens enter the host, sensing of environmental cues activates the expression of virulence genes.
evidence: This is a general statement about pathogen behavior presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this study, but is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Variability in the expression of virulence genes upon infection enhances colonization.
source: Interestingly, variability in the expression of virulence genes upon infection enhances colonization.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: EPEC exhibits bimodal growth rate upon transition from activating to non-activating conditions.
source: The analysis revealed a bimodal growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 using ScanLag methodology.

claim: The bimodality in EPEC is mediated by a hysteretic memory-switch.
source: Mathematical modeling combined with experimental analysis showed that this bimodality is mediated by a hysteretic memory-switch that results in the stable co-existence of non-virulent and hyper-virulent subpopulations, even after many generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling (Figure 3) combined with experimental observations (Figures 2, 8).

claim: The per operon is the key component of the hysteretic switch.
source: We identified the per operon as the key component of the hysteretic switch.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of perA eliminates bimodality (Figure 4) and complementation restores it (Figure 5).

claim: The hysteretic memory switch may result in persistent infection and enhanced host-to-host spreading.
source: This unique hysteretic memory switch may result in persistent infection and enhanced host-to-host spreading.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential biological significance of the findings.

claim: Bacterial populations spontaneously differentiate into distinct phenotypic states.
source: Bacterial populations spontaneously differentiate into distinct phenotypic states (Avery, 2006; Dubnau and Losick, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phenotypic variability has been described as a bet-hedging strategy that results in subpopulations that will survive under unpredictable stress.
source: This variability has been described as a bet-hedging strategy that results in subpopulations that will survive under unpredictable stress (Fraser and Kaern, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Phenotypic variability is a 'division of labor' strategy where the bacterial population diversifies to utilize nutrients more efficiently or to allow invasion and colonization of diverse niches in the host.
source: It has also been suggested that phenotypic variability is a 'division of labor' strategy: essentially, the bacterial population diversifies in order to utilize nutrients more efficiently or to allow invasion and colonization of diverse niches in the host (Ackermann et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Diversification upon infection is related to antigenic variation, which is a key strategy to eluding the acquired immune response of the host.
source: Diversification upon infection is also related to antigenic variation, which is a key strategy to eluding the acquired immune response of the host (Kamada et al., 2015; Stewart et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The role of phase-variation mechanisms in phenotypic diversification through reversible genetic changes is well established.
source: The role of phase-variation mechanisms in phenotypic diversification through reversible genetic changes is well established (see for example, Casadesús and Low, 2013; McClain et al., 1991; Silverman and Simon, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Diversification processes not linked to DNA alteration have been attributed to noise in gene expression that can be further amplified by regulatory motifs such as excitatory dynamics, positive feedback leading to bi-stability, and ultrasensitivity.
source: Diversification processes, not linked to DNA alteration have been attributed to noise in gene expression that can be further amplified by regulatory motifs such as excitatory dynamics (Süel et al., 2006) positive feedback leading to bi-stability (Ozbudak et al., 2004) and ultrasensitivity (Temme et al., 2008; Rotem et al., 2010; Levine et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Phenotypic diversification in microorganisms is frequently accompanied by growth rate variability.
source: Interestingly, phenotypic diversification in microorganisms is frequently accompanied by growth rate variability.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with an example provided.

claim: Bacterial persistence under antibiotic treatment is mediated by growth rate bimodality.
source: One striking example is that of bacterial persistence under antibiotic treatment (Lewis, 2000) mediated by growth rate bimodality (Balaban et al., 2004; Brauner et al., 2016; Helaine and Holden, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Environmental conditions that are close to those in the host environment can induce the expression of EPEC virulence genes ('activating conditions').
source: Environmental conditions that are close to those in the host environment can induce the expression of the virulence genes ('activating conditions') (Leverton and Kaper, 2005; Rosenshine et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Variability in the expression of virulence genes is observed when bacteria are exposed to activating conditions.
source: Variability in the expression of virulence genes is observed when the bacteria are exposed to activating conditions (Nielsen et al., 2010; De Angelis et al., 2011; Somvanshi et al., 2012; Atack et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Salmonella employ a type III secretion system (T3SS) to inject the host cells with virulence factors.
source: Salmonella employ a type III secretion system (T3SS) to inject the host cells with virulence factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Salmonella virulence mechanisms.

claim: Upon shifting from non-activating to activating conditions, Salmonella exhibit bimodal T3SS expression.
source: Interestingly, upon shifting from non-activating to activating conditions, Salmonella exhibit bimodal T3SS expression.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about Salmonella, with supporting context from the literature.

claim: The burden of T3SS expression, together with its bimodal expression, results in growth rate bimodality in Salmonella.
source: The burden of T3SS expression, together with its bimodal expression, results also in growth rate bimodality (Ackermann et al., 2008; Diard et al., 2013; Hautefort et al., 2003; Sturm et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The bimodality in T3SS expression provides Salmonella with a fitness advantage in the host.
source: The bimodality in the T3SS expression provides Salmonella with a fitness advantage in the host (Diard et al., 2013), contributing also to antibiotic persistence (Arnoldini et al., 2014), and to reduction in generation of non-virulent mutants termed 'defectors' (Diard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EPEC is a human specific pathogen.
source: The aim of this study was to examine whether phenotypic variability plays a role in the virulence of a model organism, enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), a human specific pathogen, during infection and in the transition to non-activating conditions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about EPEC.

claim: The major virulence factors of EPEC are a T3SS and a type IV pili termed the bundle forming pili (BFP).
source: The major virulence factors of EPEC are a T3SS, similar to that of Salmonella, and a type IV pili termed the bundle forming pili (BFP) (Gaytán et al., 2016; Hazen et al., 2016, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EPEC can cause symptoms ranging from asymptomatic infection to a devastating lethal disease in infants.
source: EPEC can cause symptoms ranging from asymptomatic infection to a devastating lethal disease in infants and spreads in the host population by the fecal-oral route (Hazen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPEC spreads in the host population by the fecal-oral route.
source: EPEC can cause symptoms ranging from asymptomatic infection to a devastating lethal disease in infants and spreads in the host population by the fecal-oral route (Hazen et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The expression of the EPEC virulence machinery is activated upon growth in DMEM at 37°C to OD600 of 0.2–0.5.
source: The expression of the EPEC virulence machinery is activated upon growth in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) at 37°C to OD600 of 0.2–0.5 ('activating conditions').
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Overnight growth in LB is considered as 'non-activating conditions' for EPEC.
source: In contrast, overnight growth in Luria-Bertani liquid medium (LB) is considered as 'non-activating conditions' (Hazen et al., 2015a; Leverton and Kaper, 2005; Puente et al., 1996; Rosenshine et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: EPEC and K-12 from overnight LB cultures displayed unimodal distributions of colony appearance times.
source: Analysis of the colony growth dynamics, using ScanLag (Levin-Reisman et al., 2010) scanners, showed that EPEC and K-12 from the overnight LB cultures displayed unimodal distributions of colony appearance times (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Colonies of EPEC that originated from activating culture conditions exhibited a bimodal distribution of appearance time.
source: In contrast, colonies of EPEC that originated from activating culture conditions exhibited a bimodal distribution of appearance time (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1); the 'activated' K-12 culture maintained a unimodal distribution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The 'activated' K-12 culture maintained a unimodal distribution of colony appearance time.
source: In contrast, colonies of EPEC that originated from activating culture conditions exhibited a bimodal distribution of appearance time (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1); the 'activated' K-12 culture maintained a unimodal distribution (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The bimodality in EPEC colony appearance time was due to a slightly reduced growth rate of the bacteria in the late-appearing colonies.
source: Further analysis showed that the bimodality in EPEC colony appearance time was due to a slightly reduced growth rate of the bacteria in the late-appearing colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in growth rates resulted in bimodal colony size distribution at 17 hr post-plating.
source: These differences in the growth rates resulted in bimodal colony size distribution at 17 hr post-plating (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Most SMALL colony bacteria gave rise to SMALL colonies (96% ± 3%).
source: Most SMALL colony bacteria gave rise to SMALL colonies (96% ± 3%; mean ± s.d.) (Figure 2B,D), whereas the bacteria originated from BIG colonies gave rise to bimodal distribution in colony size with 79% ± 4% BIG and 21% ± 4% SMALL colonies (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,D with statistical measurements.

claim: Bacteria originated from BIG colonies gave rise to bimodal distribution in colony size with 79% ± 4% BIG and 21% ± 4% SMALL colonies.
source: Most SMALL colony bacteria gave rise to SMALL colonies (96% ± 3%; mean ± s.d.) (Figure 2B,D), whereas the bacteria originated from BIG colonies gave rise to bimodal distribution in colony size with 79% ± 4% BIG and 21% ± 4% SMALL colonies (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,E with statistical measurements.

claim: Repeating the re-plating procedure for four consecutive cycles resulted in similar ratios of BIG to SMALL colonies.
source: Remarkably, repeating this procedure for four consecutive cycles resulted in similar ratios of BIG to SMALL colonies (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The memory of the SMALL phenotype is inherited for tens of generations.
source: These findings suggested that the memory of the SMALL phenotype is inherited for tens of generations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing stability over multiple cycles.

claim: The genome sequences of SMALL and BIG colonies were identical and very close to that of the published reference sequence of EPEC strain E2348/69.
source: The genome sequences of SMALL and BIG colonies were identical and very close to that of the published reference sequence of EPEC strain E2348/69 (Iguchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data.

claim: Three loci were undergoing active phase variation by DNA inversion in EPEC.
source: More advanced analysis, using a custom algorithm for the detection of DNA rearrangements typical to phase variation, identified three loci that were undergoing active phase variation by DNA inversion (Goldberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: No specific differences in phase variation regions were detected between the BIG and SMALL genomes.
source: However, we did not detect any specific differences in these regions between the BIG and SMALL genomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis data.

claim: The only significant difference between the BIG and SMALL genomes was an approximately two-fold lower coverage of pMAR2 (EAF plasmid) in the BIG variant genome relative to the SMALL genome.
source: The only significant difference between the two genomes was an approximately two-fold lower coverage of pMAR2 (EAF plasmid, Iguchi et al., 2009) in the BIG variant genome relative to the SMALL genome (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: Genetic changes are not involved in the colony size bimodality.
source: These results suggest that genetic changes are not involved in the colony size bimodality, favoring the possibility that the morphotypes are produced through an epigenetic mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic sequencing results showing no genetic differences.

claim: The morphotypes are produced through an epigenetic mechanism.
source: These results suggest that genetic changes are not involved in the colony size bimodality, favoring the possibility that the morphotypes are produced through an epigenetic mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of genetic differences between morphotypes.

claim: Growth to stationary phase may affect the SMALL morphotype memory.
source: We noticed a reduction in the SMALL morphotype inheritability when SMALL colonies were grown for more than 24 hr, before suspending and re-plating, suggesting that growth to stationary phase may affect the SMALL morphotype memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: When SMALL or BIG colonies were resuspended and grown in LB broth to stationary phase and then plated, the SMALL morphotype disappeared in both cases.
source: To test this prediction, SMALL or BIG colonies were resuspended and grown in LB broth to stationary phase and then plated and analyzed. In both cases the SMALL morphotype disappeared (Figure 2F–H), and the culture was 'reset' to form the unimodal colony-size distribution typical of that reported for stationary-phase cultures (Figure 1A, Levin-Reisman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: The SMALL morphotype is extremely stable during growth, but disappears in stationary phase cultures.
source: Taken together, these results show that the SMALL morphotype is extremely stable during growth, but disappears in stationary phase cultures.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from Figure 2.

claim: Upon growth in non-activating conditions, the switching rate from BIG to SMALL is about 10 times higher than from SMALL to BIG.
source: The model reproduced our experimental observations and suggested that upon growth in non-activating conditions, the switching rate from BIG to SMALL is about 10 times higher than from SMALL to BIG, resulting in a stable co-existence of the two morphotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical modeling fitted to experimental data.

claim: The time scale of the switching from SMALL to BIG was extremely long, requiring more than 100 hr and many generations to reach steady state.
source: Furthermore, the time scale of the switching from SMALL to BIG was extremely long, requiring more than 100 hr and many generations to reach steady state (see Materials and methods-Mathematical model).
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical modeling.

claim: Longer exposure to activating conditions would lead to a higher percentage of the SMALL morphotype.
source: Our model predicted that longer exposure to activating conditions would lead to a higher percentage of the SMALL morphotype.
evidence: This is a prediction from the mathematical model.

claim: The switching from BIG to SMALL was tenfold faster under activating conditions than under non-activating conditions.
source: We found that the switching from BIG to SMALL was tenfold faster under activating conditions than under non-activating conditions (Figure 3B and Materials and methods-Mathematical model).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and mathematical modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Within a few hours under activating conditions, the SMALL morphotype dominated the culture.
source: As a result, within a few hours under activating conditions, the SMALL morphotype dominated the culture.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and modeling results.

claim: Stationary phase resets the culture to a unimodal BIG population in both activating and non-activating conditions.
source: Similarly to growth in LB, stationary phase resets the culture to unimodality (Figure 3B,C). Taken together, these results show that although the bimodal switch generates variability both under activating and non-activating conditions, the higher switching rate under activating conditions results in a fast increase of the SMALL to BIG ratio. In both conditions, stationary phase resets the culture to a unimodal BIG population.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Ler and GrlA are not required for the bimodal colony size phenotype.
source: We tested for possible involvement of these regulators in the BIG to SMALL switch and found that Ler and GrlA are not required for the bimodal colony size phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The EPEC strain cured of the EAF plasmid lost the capacity to generate bimodality and produced only BIG colonies.
source: In contrast, the EPEC strain cured of the EAF plasmid, which encodes the perABC operon, lost the capacity to generate bimodality and produced only BIG colonies (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Complementing the EAF plasmid-cured strain with the EAF plasmid restored the bimodal phenotype.
source: Complementing this strain with the EAF plasmid restored the bimodal phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Only the ΔperA mutant failed to exhibit bimodality among the tested mutants.
source: To identify the EAF plasmid genes required to establish the bimodality, we examine mutant strains ΔperA, ΔperC, and ΔbfpA (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). Notably, only the ΔperA mutant failed to exhibit bimodality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PerA is the autoactivator and the perA mutant is deficient in expressing the entire perABC operon.
source: Importantly, PerA is the autoactivator and thus the perA mutant is deficient in expressing the entire perABC operon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PerA regulatory function.

claim: Complementing the ΔperA strain with a plasmid containing the perABC operon restored the bimodality.
source: Complementing the ΔperA strain with a low copy number plasmid, containing the perABC operon with its native regulatory region transcriptionally fused to gfp (pPerABC-GFP)restored the bimodality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The per operon is required for the co-existence of the BIG and SMALL morphotypes.
source: These results show that the per operon is required for the co-existence of the BIG and SMALL morphotypes, whereas PerC, GrlA, Ler, T3SS biogenesis, and BFP formation were not required for colony size bimodality (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: PerC, GrlA, Ler, T3SS biogenesis, and BFP formation were not required for colony size bimodality.
source: These results show that the per operon is required for the co-existence of the BIG and SMALL morphotypes, whereas PerC, GrlA, Ler, T3SS biogenesis, and BFP formation were not required for colony size bimodality (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Complementation of ΔperA with PerA-GFP or PerB-GFP expressing plasmids resulted in unimodal colony morphotypes.
source: Whereas complementation of ΔperA with PerA-GFP or PerB-GFP expressing plasmids resulted in unimodal colony morphotypes (Figure 5A), the PerAB-GFP plasmid restored bimodality, indicating that both PerA and PerB are required for the bimodality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The PerAB-GFP plasmid restored bimodality, indicating that both PerA and PerB are required for the bimodality.
source: Whereas complementation of ΔperA with PerA-GFP or PerB-GFP expressing plasmids resulted in unimodal colony morphotypes (Figure 5A), the PerAB-GFP plasmid restored bimodality, indicating that both PerA and PerB are required for the bimodality.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: GFP expression is bimodal in pPerAB-GFP plasmids, while uniformly high in pPerA-GFP.
source: Microscopic observations show that GFP expression is bimodal in pPerAB-GFP plasmids, while uniformly high in pPerA-GFP (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Co-expression of PerA and PerB is sufficient for induction of bimodality in E. coli K-12 MG1655 strain.
source: To determine whether other EAF plasmid factors are required for the growth bimodality, we transformed E. Coli K-12 MG1655 strain with the above pPer plasmids and found that co-expression of PerA and PerB is sufficient for induction of bimodality also in this strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transformation experiments.

claim: PerA or PerB alone failed to generate bimodality in E. coli K-12.
source: In agreement with the results obtained in the ΔperA EPEC strain, PerA or PerB alone failed to generate bimodality (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PerAB expression generates a bimodality of growth also without the EAF plasmid, although the phenotype was milder.
source: These results show that PerAB expression generates a bimodality of growth also without the EAF plasmid, although the phenotype was milder (i.e. the growth difference between the two morphotypes is smaller) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: During growth in activating conditions, a bimodal expression of the perABC operon is established in progenitor cells.
source: We subjected a culture of the ΔperA EPEC complemented with pPerABC-GFP to activating conditions and measured GFP expression by microscopy (Figure 6A). We detected a bimodal expression of the perABC-gfp operon.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Bacteria that did not express GFP (perABC) were larger and divided more rapidly than those that expressed GFP.
source: Furthermore, the bacteria that did not express GFP were larger and divided more rapidly than those that expressed GFP.
evidence: This is based on microscopic observations.

claim: The GFP-OFF bacteria grew in BIG colonies, whereas the GFP-ON bacteria generated almost exclusively SMALL colonies.
source: The results showed that the GFP-OFF bacteria grew in BIG colonies, whereas the GFP-ON bacteria generated almost exclusively SMALL colonies.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS sorting and ScanLag analysis data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: The bimodal expression of the perABC operon during growth in activating conditions leads to bimodality in colony size upon plating and growth in non-activating conditions.
source: Taken together, these results show that during growth in activating conditions, a bimodal expression of the perABC operon is established in progenitor cells that lead to bimodality in colony size upon plating and growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from Figure 6.

claim: Under activating conditions, Ler expression from chromosomal ler-gfp transcriptional fusion was unimodal.
source: Under activating conditions, we observed that Ler expression from chromosomal ler-gfp transcriptional fusion was unimodal (Figure 7A–C), as previously reported (Berdichevsky et al., 2005; Roe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C and citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon shifting from activating to non-activating conditions, Ler-GFP expression was reduced in approximately 50% of the bacterial population and became bimodal.
source: As predicted, we found that upon shifting from activating to non-activating conditions, Ler-GFP expression was reduced in approximately 50% of the bacterial population and became bimodal (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B,D.

claim: Ler expression was uniformly high in the SMALL population but bimodal in the BIG population.
source: Time-lapse microscopy of bacteria taken from BIG and SMALL colonies showed that, as expected, Ler expression was uniformly high in the SMALL population but bimodal in the BIG population (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bimodal expression of perABC during activating conditions does not result in bimodal Ler expression since GrlA activates ler expression regardless of whether PerC is expressed or not.
source: These results suggest that the bimodal expression from perABC during activating conditions does not result in bimodal Ler expression since GrlA, which is redundant to PerC, activates ler expression regardless of whether PerC is expressed or not.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and knowledge of the regulatory network.

claim: Upon shifting to non-activating conditions, the bimodal expression of perABC drives the bimodality of Ler expression.
source: However, upon shifting to non-activating conditions and the bimodal expression of perABC drives the bimodality of Ler expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: The entire EPEC population switches to a virulent state upon activation, characterized by unimodal and high ler expression.
source: Accordingly, the entire population switches to a virulent state upon activation, characterized by unimodal and high ler expression (Figure 8A, State 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7 and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: Per expression during activation is typically bimodal.
source: In contrast, per expression during activation is typically bimodal, although prolonged activation eventually shifts the population to SMALL (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 6.

claim: When transferred to non-activating conditions, the per-ON bacteria remain hypervirulent, expressing both Ler and PerABC, leading to SMALL colony morphotype.
source: When transferred to non-activating conditions, the per-ON bacteria remain hypervirulent, expressing both Ler and PerABC, leading to SMALL colony morphotype (Figure 8, State 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The hypervirulent state is maintained for an extremely long time but is 'reset' to the non-virulent state during stationary phase.
source: This hypervirulent state is maintained for an extremely long time but is 'reset' to the non-virulent state during stationary phase (Figure 8, State 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 2 and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The SMALL morphotype should express virulence factors downstream of both ler and per (i.e., BFP and T3SS), even after many generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
source: Firstly, the SMALL morphotype should express virulence factors downstream of both ler and per (i.e., BFP and T3SS), even after many generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hysteretic switch model.

claim: The BIG colony morphotype should consist mainly of non-virulent bacteria with ~20% of hypervirulent ones.
source: Secondly, the BIG colony morphotype should consist mainly of non-virulent bacteria with ~20% of hypervirulent ones.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the observed switching rates.

claim: The deletion of the per operon should not prevent the activation of virulence but should erase the hysteretic switch.
source: Finally, the deletion of the per operon should not prevent the activation of virulence (i.e., T3SS expression can be driven through the GrlA-Ler path), but erase the hysteretic switch, and thus ler expression and virulence of all bacteria, should decline as soon as the ΔperA bacteria are transferred to non-activating conditions (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the understanding of the regulatory network.

claim: In EPEC, EspB, Tir, and BfpA, but not FliC were highly expressed upon growth in activating conditions.
source: As expected, in EPEC, EspB, Tir, and BfpA, but not FliC were highly expressed upon growth in activating conditions (Figure 8A,C: State 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: SMALL colony bacteria showed similar expression patterns to activated bacteria despite at least 20 generations having passed since the transition from activating to non-activating conditions.
source: Similar expression patterns were seen in SMALL colony bacteria, despite the fact that at least 20 generations had passed since the transition from activating to non-activating conditions (Figure 8A,C: State 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Bacteria from BIG colonies showed low expression levels of all virulence factors and high levels of FliC.
source: In contrast, bacteria from BIG colonies showed low expression levels of all virulence factors and high levels of FliC.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The residual expression of BfpA, EspB, and Tir by the BIG colony bacteria is consistent with ~20% SMALL variants in the BIG population.
source: The residual expression of BfpA, EspB, and Tir by the BIG colony bacteria is consistent with the prediction of ~20% SMALL variants in the BIG population (Figure 8A,C: State 4).
evidence: This is an inference based on Western blot data and the known switching rates.

claim: The ΔperA mutant showed high expression of EspB and Tir when grown in activating conditions.
source: Finally, the ΔperA mutant showed high expression of EspB and Tir when grown in activating conditions, consistent with activation of ler expression by GrlA (Figure 8B,D: State 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Expression of EspB and Tir rapidly diminished when the ΔperA mutant culture was shifted to growth under non-activating conditions.
source: However, expression of these proteins rapidly diminished when the mutant culture was shifted to growth under non-activating conditions (Figure 8B,D: State 4), leading to a pattern expected from a unimodal non-virulent population (i.e., high FliC, low EspB and low Tir) and similar to the pattern of expression in the stationary phase LB culture (Figure 8A,C: State 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Resuspended SMALL colony bacteria rapidly aggregated, whereas BIG colony bacteria remained mostly planktonic.
source: Time-lapse microscopy showed that, as expected, resuspended SMALL colony bacteria rapidly aggregated, whereas BIG colony bacteria remained mostly planktonic (Figure 9A, Video 1 (BIG), Video 2 (SMALL), Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 9A and videos.

claim: The aggregates disintegrated upon reaching stationary phase, consistent with the resetting of colony-size bimodality.
source: In both cases, the aggregates disintegrated upon reaching stationary phase, consistent with the resetting of colony-size bimodality (Figure 2F–H) and the significant reduction in BfpA production in stationary phase (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations and Western blot data.

claim: The bacteria that expressed PerABC (GFP-ON, per-ON) formed microcolonies that rapidly attached to the epithelial cells.
source: The results showed that the bacteria that expressed PerABC (GFP-ON, per-ON) formed microcolonies that rapidly attached to the epithelial cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The GFP-OFF (per-OFF) bacteria remained mostly planktonic and unattached during HeLa cell infection.
source: In contrast, the GFP-OFF (per-OFF) bacteria remained mostly planktonic and unattached.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The per-ON bacteria, which generate the SMALL colony morphotype, display higher infectivity than per-OFF bacteria.
source: These results show that the per-ON bacteria, which generate the SMALL colony morphotype, display higher infectivity than per-OFF bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the infection experiments shown in Figure 9B.

claim: During the first hours of infection, the SMALL bacteria formed aggregates (microcolonies) and almost no planktonic single bacteria were found in the surrounding medium.
source: During the first hours of infection, the SMALL bacteria formed aggregates (microcolonies) and almost no planktonic single bacteria were found in the surrounding medium (Figure 9C–E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 9C-E and videos.

claim: SMALL microcolonies attached to host cells, induced actin rearrangement in the host, and invaded into the host cell.
source: Furthermore, these SMALL microcolonies attached to host cells, an indication of BFP function (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), induced actin rearrangement in the host, and invaded into the host cell, indicatives of T3SS functionality (Figure 9—figure supplement 2, Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and gentamicin protection assay data shown in Figure 9 supplements.

claim: Only a few bacteria that originated from BIG colonies were organized into attached microcolonies, and formation of actin rearrangement as well as invasiveness were marginal.
source: In contrast, only a few bacteria that originated from BIG colonies were organized into attached microcolonies, and formation of actin rearrengement as well as invasiveness were marginal (Figure 9C–E, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B, Videos 3 and 4, Figure 9—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and infection assay data shown in Figure 9 and supplements.

claim: The SMALL morphotype maintains high infectivity and expresses functional BFP and T3SS even after many generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
source: These results show that the SMALL morphotype maintains high infectivity and expresses functional BFP and T3SS even after many generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the infection experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The virulence machinery of EPEC is controlled by a hysteretic switch with long epigenetic memory.
source: This study showed, for the first time to our knowledge, that the virulence machinery of a human pathogen, EPEC, is controlled by a hysteretic switch with long epigenetic memory.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data and modeling.

claim: PerA and PerB are sufficient for the hysteretic switch.
source: We showed that PerA and PerB are sufficient for this hysteretic switch.
evidence: This claim is supported by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: When exposed to virulence-activating conditions all EPEC bacteria upregulate expression of T3SS virulence genes, unlike the bimodal virulence expression observed in Salmonella.
source: We found that when exposed to virulence-activating conditions all EPEC bacteria upregulate expression of T3SS virulence genes, unlike the bimodal virulence expression observed in Salmonella.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 7 and comparison with literature on Salmonella.

claim: The EPEC virulent population is bimodal for expression of the per regulated genes, resulting in two coexisting virulent sub-populations of bacteria, planktonic (per-OFF) and aggregative (per-ON).
source: However, we found that the EPEC virulent population is bimodal for expression of the per regulated genes, resulting in two coexisting virulent sub-populations of bacteria, planktonic (per-OFF) and aggregative (per-ON), with different infection and invasion abilities.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data from Figures 6 and 9.

claim: The per-ON population constitutively expresses both BFP and T3SS for many generations, rapidly attaches to host cells as microcolonies, delivers effectors into the host cell, and invades it.
source: The latter population constitutively expresses both BFP and T3SS for many generations, rapidly attaches to host cells as microcolonies, delivers effectors into the host cell, and invades it.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Rapid invasion may protect the bacteria against the host immune system and establish persistent infection.
source: This rapid invasion may protect the bacteria against the host immune system and establish persistent infection (Tuchscherr et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The per-OFF bacteria no longer express ler regulated genes upon transfer to non-activating conditions.
source: Whereas the per-OFF bacteria no longer express ler regulated genes upon transfer to non-activating conditions, the per-ON bacteria maintain high expression of the ler regulated virulence genes even after tens of generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The per-ON bacteria maintain high expression of the ler regulated virulence genes even after tens of generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
source: Whereas the per-OFF bacteria no longer express ler regulated genes upon transfer to non-activating conditions, the per-ON bacteria maintain high expression of the ler regulated virulence genes even after tens of generations of growth in non-activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The per-ON long-term memory may allow the pathogen to overcome transit through niches of non-activating conditions without a drop in virulence level.
source: This per-ON long-term memory may allow the pathogen to overcome transit through niches of non-activating conditions without a drop in virulence level.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the biological significance of the findings.

claim: An extreme case of transit through non-activating conditions is the host-to-host transit through the fecal-oral route.
source: An extreme case of this type of transit is the host-to-host transit through the fecal-oral route.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of EPEC transmission.

claim: The long-term memory per-ON state may set the stage for further diversification within this subpopulation, possibly creating a range of infective phenotypes.
source: In addition, the long-term memory per-ON state may set the stage for further diversification within this subpopulation, possibly creating a range of infective phenotypes, each adapted to a different niche and/or stage of infection within the host intestine.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential consequences of the hysteretic switch.

claim: The hysteretic switch that enables the coexistence of two different phenotypes may be attributable to bet-hedging in the absence of a predictable environment.
source: Alternatively, the hysteretic switch that enables the coexistence of two different phenotypes may be attributable to bet-hedging (i.e. to risk spreading in the absence of a predictable environment).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claim: The SMALL morphotype infects host cells more rapidly but bears the cost of expressing virulence genes and exposure to the immune system.
source: The SMALL morphotype infects host cells more rapidly but bears the cost of expressing virulence genes and exposure to the immune system, whereas the BIG morphotype grows faster and is less immunogenic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and general knowledge of bacterial virulence.

claim: The BIG morphotype grows faster and is less immunogenic.
source: The SMALL morphotype infects host cells more rapidly but bears the cost of expressing virulence genes and exposure to the immune system, whereas the BIG morphotype grows faster and is less immunogenic.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations showing faster growth and lower virulence gene expression.

claim: Bimodality is stable mainly under non-activating conditions.
source: Notably, bimodality is stable mainly under non-activating conditions, suggesting that insufficient cues from the environment regarding bacterial residence inside or outside the host may promote a bet-hedging strategy (Kussell and Leibler, 2005).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PerA is central for the hysteretic switch.
source: We found that PerA is central for this switch and that the PerA-regulated perABC operon exhibits bimodal expression when co-expressed with PerB.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The per operon is regulated by PerA auto-activation, a network motif that has been shown to lead to bimodality and hysteresis.
source: Notably, the per operon is regulated by PerA auto-activation (Figure 4A), a network motif that has been shown to lead to bimodality (Smits et al., 2006) and hysteresis (Mitrophanov and Groisman, 2008), which can lead to bistability by growth feedback mechanisms (Deris et al., 2013; Irwin et al., 2010; Tan et al., 2009), or other mechanisms, for which PerB may be required.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on regulatory network motifs.

claim: Specific environmental conditions strongly increased the per-ON frequency in the population by enhancing the switching rate by a factor of ~10 compared to non-activating conditions.
source: Specific environmental conditions (termed here 'activating conditions') strongly increased the per-ON frequency in the population by enhancing the switching rate by a factor of ~10 compared to non-activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling and experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Growth under activating conditions resulted in almost 100% of per-ON cells at steady state.
source: Thus, growth under activating conditions resulted in almost 100% of per-ON cells at steady state.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and modeling shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Per expression is essential for establishing a hysteretic long-term memory switch.
source: Importantly, our results show that per expression is essential for establishing a hysteretic long-term memory switch, resulting in the co-existence of per-OFF and per-ON subpopulations, of which the latter remains stable even in the face of drastic changes in the environmental conditions, such as shifts in temperature and growth media.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data.

claim: A single bacterium in the per-ON state generates a colony of the SMALL morphotype in which most of the bacteria remain per-ON and are primed for rapid infection of host cells.
source: Given this stability, a single bacterium in the per-ON state generates a colony of the SMALL morphotype in which most of the bacteria remain per-ON and are primed for rapid infection of host cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of colony inheritance patterns.

claim: The per-ON memory vanished once growth reaches stationary phase, and the entire population switched to per-OFF.
source: Interestingly, the per-ON memory vanished once growth reaches stationary phase, and the entire population switched to per-OFF.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: In EPEC, expression of the Ler master regulator, and thus expression of T3SS, is high and unimodal under activating conditions.
source: In EPEC, expression of the Ler master regulator, and thus expression of T3SS, is high and unimodal under activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Redundant activation of the ler promoter by independent regulators (GrlA and PerC) ensures that all bacteria express virulent genes during activation.
source: Redundant activation of the ler promoter by independent regulators (GrlA and PerC) ensures that all bacteria express virulent genes during activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of the regulatory network and experimental observations.

claim: In Salmonella, ler expression becomes bimodal only when the bacteria are transferred to non-activating conditions.
source: Thus in EPEC, ler expression becomes bimodal only when the bacteria are transferred to non-activating conditions, resulting in the co-existence of non-activated bacteria and bacteria that are already primed for infection through constitutive expression of BFP and T3SS.
evidence: This is stated in contrast to EPEC behavior, implying knowledge about Salmonella from the literature.

claim: The rate of switching from ON to OFF in EPEC is extremely slow (several weeks), even under non-activating conditions.
source: Importantly, we were able to evaluate the rates of switching between the two EPEC phenotypes and found that the rate from ON to OFF is extremely slow (several weeks), even under non-activating conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on mathematical modeling fitted to experimental data.

claim: A long-lived ON state has been observed in Salmonella.
source: A long-lived ON state has been observed also in Salmonella (Sturm et al., 2011), but upon shifting to non-activating conditions, regulators of virulence decay within 1 to 2 hr (Temme et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Salmonella.

claim: In Salmonella, upon shifting to non-activating conditions, regulators of virulence decay within 1 to 2 hr.
source: A long-lived ON state has been observed also in Salmonella (Sturm et al., 2011), but upon shifting to non-activating conditions, regulators of virulence decay within 1 to 2 hr (Temme et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The importance of the hysteretic switch for EPEC virulence is reflected by the conservation of the switch core: the perABC operon.
source: The importance of the described hysteretic switch for EPEC virulence is reflected by the conservation of the switch core: the perABC operon.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic analysis of EPEC strains.

claim: EPEC is an umbrella name for a collection of E. coli strains belonging to diverse phylogenetic branches that acquired independently, through horizontal gene transfer, a pathogenicity island encoding T3SS (the LEE island).
source: Recent reports comparing the genome sequences of a large number of EPEC clinical isolates show that EPEC is an umbrella name for a collection of E. coli strains belonging to diverse phylogenetic branches that acquired independently, through horizontal gene transfer, a pathogenicity island encoding T3SS (the LEE island) (Ingle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Most EPEC strains also acquired plasmids containing the perABC operon.
source: Notably, most of these EPEC strains also acquired plasmids containing the perABC operon (Ingle et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Strains containing both the LEE and plasmids encoding perABC and bfp operons cause a more severe disease.
source: Furthermore, strains containing both the LEE and plasmids encoding perABC and bfp operons cause a more severe disease (Hazen et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The contribution of PerA might be related to regulation of additional virulence-related genes.
source: Hazen et al. proposed that the contribution of PerA might be related to regulation of additional virulence-related genes (Hazen et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is a proposal from previous literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: perABC enhances the fitness of infecting EPEC by facilitating formation of long-term memory and stable phenotypic bimodality.
source: Our findings suggest that perABC also enhances the fitness of infecting EPEC by facilitating formation of long-term memory and stable phenotypic bimodality.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of this study.

claim: The contribution of the per-switch to virulence in vivo could not be tested since an animal model for EPEC is not available.
source: The contribution of the per-switch to virulence in vivo could not be tested since an animal model for EPEC is not available.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: Pathogens closely related to EPEC, including EHEC and Citrobacter rodentium, do not carry the perABC operon.
source: Pathogens closely related to EPEC, including enterohemorragic E. coli (EHEC) and Citrobacter rodentium (CR), do not carry the perABC operon.
evidence: This is established knowledge about related pathogens.

claim: Heterogeneity in virulence is observed in EHEC and Citrobacter rodentium.
source: Interestingly, however, heterogeneity in virulence is observed in these pathogens (Roe et al., 2004; Kamada et al., 2015), but the involved switch and whether it is also hysteretic have not been studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A hysteretic switch controls the virulence traits of EPEC.
source: In conclusion, we report here how a hysteretic switch controls the virulence traits of a human pathogen, EPEC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: This understanding may lead to the development of new strategies to interfere with the establishment of stable virulence-ON mechanisms and thus reduce virulence and pathogen spreading to new hosts.
source: Furthermore, this understanding may lead to the development of new strategies to interfere with the establishment of stable virulence-ON mechanisms and thus reduce virulence and pathogen spreading to new hosts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the findings.

claim: It is likely that this hysteretic switch is common in pathogenic bacteria, ensuring persistence of infection and improved host-to-host spreading.
source: It is likely that this hysteretic switch is common in pathogenic bacteria, ensuring persistence of infection and improved host-to-host spreading.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader significance of the findings.
